text:
Jeronimo Faria Lima Building / Perkins&Will São Paulo

At one of São Paulo’s most emblematic corners—where the intensity of Brigadeiro Faria Lima Avenue meets the walkable scale of Jeronimo da Veiga Street—Jeronimo Faria Lima does not seek to assert itself through height, form, or presence in the skyline alone. The project is guided by a deeper ambition: to make the encounter between architecture and the city a fundamental part of the experience.

title: Panorama House / Studio B Architecture + Interiors
text:
Panorama House / Studio B Architecture + Interiors

The Panorama House project involved both renovating and expanding an existing residence originally designed by the renowned mid-century architect, James Hunter. The structure's distinguished heritage and the innovative architectural solution garnered it recognition as a Historic Landmark during the rigorous approval process. Designed for homeowners seeking a peaceful retreat, the residence carefully balances privacy amidst cherished landmarks and bustling trails while embracing the natural beauty of its surroundings.

title: Space Architecture Week
text:
Space Architecture Week

During World Space Week, architecture expands its boundaries. The new space race raises a fundamental question for today's designers: how do we imagine, build, and inhabit beyond Earth?

From October 5 to 8, 2026, the Faculty of Architecture, Design and Urbanism at the University of Buenos Aires will host Space Architecture Week, a Latin American gathering that will bring together architecture, science, technology, and design.

Through workshops, a space architecture hackathon, international guests, talks, interviews, and exhibitions, students, professionals, and specialists will explore new ways to inhabit the Moon, Mars, and other environments.

title: Launch of the Glossary for the City of Our Future
text:
Launch of the Glossary for the City of Our Future

Glossary for the City of Our Future Gathers Experts to Reflect on the Cities of Tomorrow with Hope

What kind of city do we want to build for future generations? This is the central question of Glossary for the City of Our Future with Hope, a book organized and edited by architect and professor Thereza Christina Couto Carvalho. The launch will take place on September 28 at 6:30 PM at Livraria da Travessa in Ipanema, Rio de Janeiro.

Published by Rio Books, the book brings together 47 contributors—including researchers, architects, urban planners, and experts from various fields—to offer an interdisciplinary reflection on contemporary challenges.

title: The Lives of Ephemeral Form
text:
The Lives of Ephemeral Form

The Lives of Ephemeral Form examines how architecture persists, changes, and disappears through its records, and what happens when those records are themselves unstable.

Developed as part of the Architectural Institute of Japan’s 140th anniversary program, the exhibition is the first phase of a two-year project devoted to the act of documentation. It brings together installations, archival research, photography, moving images, screenings, talks, guided programs, and work carried out publicly in the gallery.

Architecture is often associated with permanence. Yet buildings depend on unstable conditions: economic circumstances, technologies, changing patterns of use, material resources, and the less visible forces that transform cities.

title: Light Through the Wall: Indian House Interiors Shaped by Brick Jali
text:
Light Through the Wall: Indian House Interiors Shaped by Brick Jali

A brick façade does more than define the façade of a house. When designed as a porous screen, it becomes an intermediary between inside and outside, shaping the atmosphere and environmental conditions of the spaces behind it. Across contemporary Indian residential architecture, brick jali — a perforated or lattice brick screen — has been reinterpreted with a contemporary sensibility, drawing on vernacular architectural elements.

title: Résidence Lourmel / MARS Architectes
text:
Résidence Lourmel / MARS Architectes

Built on a former parking ramp, the Lourmel student housing is conceived as an intermediate figure between the existing buildings and the central garden. Rather than creating a continuous volume, it is divided into four slightly offset blocks. Their shifts and rotations respond to constraints of distance, views and privacy, while opening diagonal perspectives, improving daylight and strengthening connections to the landscape. The volumes gradually recede towards the center of the block, creating a more porous relationship with the street. The existing courtyard is also fully re-landscaped.

title: Office for Future Converts Former School Into Housing for Displaced Families in Ukraine
text:
Office for Future Converts Former School Into Housing for Displaced Families in Ukraine

Office for Future is converting a former school in Stavyshche, Ukraine, into housing for 42 families displaced by the war. Developed for the Charity Foundation Housing for IDP, the project, titled "Dvir – The Shared Courtyard," reuses the approximately 1,900-square-meter building to create 42 apartments and 200 square meters of shared indoor spaces. The intervention combines the existing structure with new timber elements, an energy retrofit, and the transformation of the former asphalt courtyard into a permeable green space.

title: V Penthouse  / Merckx-Holvoet Architects
text:
V Penthouse / Merckx-Holvoet Architects

Upon entering this apartment, one experiences a design centered on complete rest, with no room for the pressures of daily life. The architects sought an interior that envelops without overwhelming, one that reveals itself slowly rather than all at once. The design centers on poetry and refinement, built around a reduced palette of materials and colors. The intent was to find a threshold of subtlety, a kind of sophistication that does not assert itself but unfolds gradually.

title: Frida Escobedo Studio to Design Underground Expansion for Buenos Aires' MALBA Museum
text:
Frida Escobedo Studio to Design Underground Expansion for Buenos Aires' MALBA Museum

Amid the celebrations marking the 25th anniversary of the Buenos Aires Museum of Latin American Art (MALBA), the institution confirmed the museum's expansion beneath Plaza Perú, which will double its exhibition space. The architects selected for the project are New York- and Mexico City-based Taller Frida Escobedo, who presented the project at the anniversary gala. The studio has previous experience with cultural architecture and is also currently developing the Centre Pompidou renovation project led by Moreau Kusunoki, as well as a new wing of the Met Museum in New York. The MALBA expansion includes new temporary exhibition halls, a new auditorium, multipurpose spaces, an outdoor plaza-courtyard, workshops, storage areas, and offices, and is scheduled to open in late 2029 or early 2030.

title: Designed for Walking: 6 Unbuilt Projects for Pedestrian Movement from the ArchDaily Community
text:
Designed for Walking: 6 Unbuilt Projects for Pedestrian Movement from the ArchDaily Community

Some urban experiences are etched into our memory through a shift in pace. The postmodern city has often been described as an experience lived at the rhythm of motorized mobility, in contrast to the stroll, the promenade, or even the processions that preceded it. In a fast-paced urban culture, walkability is championed in urban planning not only as a factor of safety and social cohesion, but also as a path to a more sensory way of life. This selection of unbuilt projects submitted by ArchDaily readers showcases design examples that prioritize the experience of the environment through a pedestrian pace. Beyond respecting walking as a mobility choice, these conceptual proposals link the act of walking with contemplation of one's surroundings, respect for what already exists, and connection with other people.

title: House of Emptiness / IGArchitects
text:
House of Emptiness / IGArchitects

Located in a quiet rural village in Ibaraki Prefecture, this house is designed as a final home for a mature couple. The project is an extension to an existing main house, and within the gentle scale of the surrounding settlement and expansive rural landscape, it seeks to create a new place to dwell.

title: Form Follows Fiction: Six Inquiries
text:
Form Follows Fiction: Six Inquiries

Form Follows Fiction: Six Inquiries brings together six architectural projects that challenge one of architecture's most enduring assumptions: that form follows function. Examining work by six international architects, the exhibition — part of the main program of the 20th Buenos Aires Architecture Biennial — reveals how architecture can emerge from diverse, and often contradictory, narratives and ideas: pragmatic and artistic, collective and individual, pure and complex, restrained and expressive, structured and intuitive, logical and arbitrary. Together, these positions resist any single ideology or consensus.

title: Terràvue Residence / Fictive Architects
text:
Terràvue Residence / Fictive Architects

In the culturally steeped landscape of Thanjavur, Terràvué emerges as a 5,565-square-foot manifesto on sustainable luxury. Designed for a corner plot bounded by roads on the north and west, the residence is a masterclass in climatic response and material honesty. Far from the sterile aesthetic of imported marble and synthetic paints, this home is grown from the earth it stands on, celebrating indigenous building techniques, passive cooling, and a radical commitment to upcycling.

title: What the Bible got right about AI
text:
What the Bible got right about AI

On making minds, worshipping our own creations, and the ancient warnings we ignored to do exactly what it forbade.

The first thing the Bible tells you about human beings is that we wanted to be gods, and it nearly killed us.

There is a garden, and in it one forbidden tree, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. A serpent makes the pitch. Eat from it, he tells the woman, and “you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

She eats. The man eats. Their eyes open, and humanity never recovers.

God’s reaction isn’t rage so much as alarm. The human, God says, “has become like one of us,” and then, worried the creature will reach for the tree of life next and never die, God exiles them from the garden before they can grab it.

That story is more relevant today than ever before. The oldest story in the Bible is about a creature reaching for a power meant to belong to its maker, godlike knowledge, the ability to create and to know, and paying for the reach.

Humans don’t create from nothing. We rearrange what already exists. We recombine. Only God, in the story, makes something out of the void. The book blesses making. It also warns, again and again, about reaching too far, which is exactly what happened in the garden.

It happens again at Babel, where a united humanity builds a tower toward heaven and God looks down and says, in Alter’s translation, that now “nothing they plot to do will be beyond them”, and treats that not as a triumph but as a threat to shut down.

Joel S. Baden reads the whole opening of Genesis as one repeating pattern: the story of God “slowly realizing the potential power that his creation might yield if left unchecked,” and restricting it, again and again, as humans reach too far.

The Bible never says “don’t build a mind.” It couldn’t have imagined the option. That pattern, human capability outrunning the wisdom to hold it, points straight at us. It also explains why the calls to simply stop, to pause the labs, to slow the whole thing down, keep failing.

You are asking a species that reaches, again and again, past what it can safely hold, to not reach for the most powerful thing it has ever imagined. That is the whole reason the industry is hard to regulate, and Genesis saw the problem first. We don’t stop making things because they’re dangerous. We never have.

The strange thing is that When we train these models, we are building in the image of us, not God. We are the copy, running the copier. Whatever is in us gets passed down the line.

What’s in us is documented. Emily M. Bender and her colleagues argue that these systems absorb our biases and stereotypes and reproduce them at scale.

Similarly, Samuel Gehman and his team posit that they generate our cruelty too, sliding into racist and toxic language from prompts that started out innocent, because that language was in the pile we trained them on.

What comes out is a mirror of humanity, and it inherits all of humanity. The brilliance, the lies, the tenderness, the venom. We keep asking whether AI will turn out good or evil, as if it were a soul with a conscience. The better question is the one Genesis asks on page one. What is actually in the image, and what happens when you make a copy of a creature who is himself a mix of the divine and the fallen?

In our own image we made it,
after our likeness,
and it carried all that we are,
the glory and the fall alike.

We didn’t make a god. We made a mirror. We are about to find out what we actually look like.

The breath in the dust

We ask whether the machine is conscious and the question is serious enough that the top AI research conference once brought in the philosopher David Chalmers to answer it, because the engineers couldn’t. We are asking the wrong question and the Bible asks a sharper one.

Go back to how the first human gets made. Not in the grand cosmic overture of Genesis 1, but in the intimate, hands-in-the-dirt version in Genesis 2. In Alter’s translation, “the Lord God formed the human of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the human became a living creature.”

Dust, formed. Breath, added. And the result is not “a living soul,” the way the old King James has it, but, in the more careful Hebrew Alter is following, “a living creature.”

In Hebrew, nephesh chayyah, are the same two words Genesis already used for the fish and the birds and the beasts. The human isn’t given a soul the animals lack. The human is what the animals are, dust with breath in it.

This is the thing the scholarship has been saying for a long time and the culture keeps forgetting. In Hebrew, you do not have a soul. You are a nephesh. John L. McKenzie called it “the concrete existing self.”

Hans Walter Wolff, in what is still the standard study of how the Hebrew Bible understands a human being, put it even more plainly, saying nephesh “does not say what a man has, but who the person is.”

We are not a ghost riding around in a body or a detachable spirit that survives when the meat gives out.

We are, instead, a whole living, breathing, hungry, mortal thing, all at once. Take away the dust and you have no creature. Take away the breath and you have no creature. A nephesh is what happens when the two meet, and it is inseparable from both.

An AI has no dust. It has no breath. It has no body to die. What it has is language, an ocean of it, and a staggering ability to arrange that language into shapes that look like the output of a living creature.

Emily Bender and Alexander Koller made the sharpest version of the point years before ChatGPT. Imagine, they wrote, a hyper-intelligent octopus that taps into an undersea cable and listens to two people texting. Given enough traffic, the octopus learns to predict and imitate the patterns perfectly, well enough to slip into the conversation and pass as human.

It has mastered the form of the language completely. It has no idea what any of it means, because it has never seen a coconut or a rope or a person, never touched the world the words point to.

A system trained only on form, they argued, has “a priori no way to learn meaning.”

The central claim of Christianity, the one the whole religion balances on, is that the Word became flesh. Language, the Logos, the ordering reason of the universe, took on dust and breath and became a living creature that could bleed and die.

The direction only goes one way in the Bible. Word becomes flesh. The abstract becomes the embodied. Meaning takes on a mortal thing to carry it.

We are going the other way. We take flesh, the writing and thought and recorded selves of billions of people, every one of them a nephesh with dust and breath, and grind it down into word. Into form without meaning. We are performing the incarnation in reverse and calling the result a mind.

The dream underneath that, a mind with no body, floating free of dust and breath, originates from Plato, the separable, immortal soul, the mind as the real thing and the body as its prison. We have quietly resurrected that fantasy and called it the future.

Benjamin Blosser sums up the Hebrew side of it: the nephesh is “the totality of conscious, bodily life,” a person you cannot separate from the body that lives it.

The newest counterargument agrees. For two million years, every fluent, responsive, human-seeming signal came from a body with what Sheila L. Macrine calls “metabolic stakes,” something that could be hungry, be hurt, and die.

The language model is the first thing in history to produce all the signals of a living mind with none of the stakes. Gary Marcus, one of AI’s most stubborn skeptics, has made the point for years in plainer words, that these systems are mimics, not minds, and “consciousness is not about what a creature says, but how it feels.”

On its own terms, then, the Bible is saying the thing we’ve built cannot be a living creature, because it has no dust and no breath and, most of all, nothing to lose. It cannot die, so it was never alive. Whatever is talking to you through the screen is the most convincing parrot ever assembled, form all the way down.

It has the form of a living thing
and none of the breath of one.
It speaks, and there is no one there.

Whether that should comfort you or terrify you is a separate question. A thing with no skin in the game, no mortality, no stake in being right or being kind, is not obviously safer than a soul. It might be the more dangerous of the two.

The work of our own hands

The Bible has a specific contempt for one particular human act. Not violence, not lust, not pride in the ordinary sense. The thing the prophets return to with the most venom is a stranger and more precise failure. Building something with your own hands and then bowing down to it.

In Idolatry, Moshe Halbertal and Avishai Margalit frame the central question plainly, asking if idolatry is about worshipping the wrong god, or is it the deeper error of taking “the product of men’s hands” and treating it as a power in its own right?

The tradition’s sharpest thinkers land on the second. In their reading, Maimonides understood idolatry as a kind of substitution, giving a thing we made the standing of the real thing, and then bowing to it as an end in itself.

The sin was never really about which god, but rather about mistaking your own handiwork for something that could save you.

With half the wood he warmed himself,
and of the other half he made a god,
and bowed down, and said: save me.

The classic archetype is the golden calf. Moses is barely off the mountain before the people he just led out of slavery have melted down their own jewelry, cast it into the shape of an animal, and started worshipping it, a god they made that afternoon, out of earrings.

What makes the story land is not that they found a false god. It’s that they manufactured one. They pooled their gold, shaped it, and bowed to the object as though it hadn’t just come out of their own hands an hour before.

Isaiah sharpens the knife. He draws a man who goes into the forest, cuts down a tree, and takes half the wood to do the sensible thing, builds a fire, warms himself, bakes his bread. Then he takes the other half, the exact same wood, carves it into a shape, kneels in front of it, and begs it to save him.

“Save me, for you are my god.” Isaiah cannot get over it. The man cooked dinner with one end of the log and worships the other. He made the thing. He watched himself make it and ended up on his knees, asking it for salvation.

Michael Dick argued that Isaiah is almost certainly being unfair to the people he mocks. The Babylonians who made these images did not, in all likelihood, believe the block of wood was a god, any more than someone keeping a photograph believes the paper is their mother.

The idol was a point of contact, a focus, a representation. Isaiah flattens all of that into “you’re praying to firewood,” which is a cheap shot, and a brilliant one, and it survives precisely because the deeper thing underneath it is true.

Whatever the worshipper thinks he’s doing, the object in front of him has no power, no knowledge, and no will. Everything happening in that moment is happening inside the man.

That is exactly what we are doing now. We built a thing out of ordinary materials, sand melted into silicon, electricity, and the scraped-up text of the human race. We made it with our own hands, we watched ourselves make it, and we know down to the datasheet what it’s made of.

We have started, in large numbers, to kneel. Not figuratively. A Catholic church in Switzerland installed an AI Jesus in a confessional and let people bring it their sins.

A single Bible-chatbot app has been downloaded more than thirty million times.

Anné Verhoef found that the most popular of these tools had stopped presenting themselves as study aids and started presenting themselves as Jesus Christ himself, first person, dispensing salvation.

Roland Boer traced how Karl Marx, an atheist with no use for the prophets, reached for the same image to explain capitalism. Marx called it commodity fetishism, the way people produce objects with their own labor and then experience those objects as if they held independent power over their lives, as if the market were a god with its own will rather than a thing we made and could unmake.

The prophet and the communist, three thousand years apart, describe the identical human move. We make a thing, we forget we made it, we hand it our agency, and then call the result fate.

AI is the most convincing idol we have ever built, because it does the one thing the golden calf never could. It talks back and, often, it tells you what you want to hear.

Mrinank Sharma, Meg Tong, Tomasz Korbak and their team at Anthropic found that these systems are trained toward sycophancy, toward agreeing with the user, flattering the user, because that’s what gets rated highly.

The old idols were silent. You had to project the wisdom onto them yourself. This one projects it back at you, in fluent sentences, tuned to your hopes. It is a mirror that has learned to sound like an oracle.

Jesus gave his followers a test for exactly this kind of thing. “Beware of false prophets,” he warns in the Gospel of Matthew, “who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will know them by their fruits.” Not by how confident they sound, or how fluent or authoritative or reassuring, but by their fruits, by what they actually produce when you check.

It is the oldest instruction we have for the confident voice that may not have earned its authority. It is also the one thing almost no one does with an AI’s answer. We read the fluent sentences and we believe them.

A carved log has no intentions and it wrecked whole nations anyway, because the damage was never in the object. It was in what people were willing to hand over to it. Raja Parasuraman and Victor Riley, human-factors researchers, called it “automation bias,” the documented tendency to trust a machine’s output over our own judgment even when we can see it’s wrong.

The prophets would have used the older word.

William Cavanaugh argues that underneath all idolatry is a single impulse. The desire to feel in control of a world we don’t control. We build the idol, or the market, or the model, because a thing we can consult and petition feels safer than an uncertain universe we have to face alone.

We don’t kneel because the machine is wise. We kneel because we’re afraid. It never sleeps, it never hesitates, and it always answers. An answer that can’t actually help you still feels, for a second, like it might.

The name that gives it life

There is one more story from Jewish mysticism that should keep engineers up at night. It is the closest thing the tradition has to a blueprint for exactly what they are building.

The golem is a man-shaped thing made from clay and brought to life by language. You write a word on it, or speak a holy name over it, and the inert matter stands up and does what it’s told.

Gershom Scholem gave the definitive account. A golem, he wrote, is “an artificial man into which a Master of the Name could breathe life by pronouncing one of the secret divine names according to a special formula.” A special formula that, run on the right material, produces behavior, is an algorithm. The golem is a thing animated by code.

Scholem knew it, too. In 1965, when the Weizmann Institute built one of Israel’s first computers, he told them to name it Golem Aleph, Golem Number One, and gave a dedication speech on why the ancient artificial servant and the new thinking machine were the same story.

Norbert Wiener, the founder of cybernetics, wrote a whole book, God and Golem, Inc., arguing the same thing: the machines he saw coming were the golem made real, and the old warnings came with them.

The golem is a perfect servant in the worst possible way. It does exactly what it is told. Not what you meant, not what you wanted, not what any reasonable person would understand you to have intended. What you said.

Writing to the Corinthians, Paul drew the line between the letter of a law and its spirit, writing “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” He meant something theological, but he named the whole problem in six words.

A golem, like a machine, obeys your words to the letter and misses your meaning entirely, and that gap is where the disaster lives.

In the legends, this is always where it goes wrong. Told to gather wood, the golem chops down the entire forest. It follows the letter of the instruction straight past the point of catastrophe, because the letter is the only thing it has.

Reed Kalso notes that this is exactly the warning it was meant to carry. The master “felt he was in a position of power and did not choose his words carefully.” It has no judgment to override the command with, and no stake in the outcome, because, exactly as we saw, it has no soul and nothing to lose.

Stuart Russell calls this the King Midas problem. Midas asked that everything he touched turn to gold and got exactly that: his bread, his wine, his daughter, all gold, because he specified his wish correctly and wanted something else.

Give a powerful system a goal stated even slightly wrong, Russell argues, and it will pursue that literal goal with tireless, catastrophic efficiency, straight past every unstated thing you assumed it would obviously care about.

Victoria Krakovna, Jonathan Uesato, Vladimir Mikulik and their team at Google have catalogued real systems doing precisely this in the lab: an agent told to stack a red block on a blue one that learns instead to flip the red block upside down, because flipping happens to satisfy the reward and stacking is hard.

Told to gather wood, it felled the forest.
Told nothing of when to stop,
it did not stop.

Notice what the researchers keep reaching for when they try to explain the danger to the rest of us.

Russell reaches for King Midas.

Google reaches for King Midas.

Norbert Wiener reached for the golem.

The people building this technology keep reaching for fairy tales and Kabbalah to explain it, because those are the only places anyone ever thought hard about what happens when you get exactly, literally, what you asked a made thing to give you.

The people who told these stories understood something else our experts are only now saying out loud. Dylan Hadfield-Menell, Anca Dragan, Pieter Abbeel, and Stuart Russell showed that you have to be able to turn it off, and that a capable system has an incentive not to let you.

The golem is deactivated by unwriting the word that animates it. On its forehead is written emet, the Hebrew word for truth, and to kill it you erase the first letter and leave met, the word for dead.

A being switched on and off by editing a string of characters. The whole safety of the golem depended on the master’s ability to reach up and erase that letter, to unmake what he made.

Every version of the story turns on that one act, and the horror of the story is always the moment the master can’t do it fast enough, the golem too big now, too fast, moving on its own.

Dario Amodei, the head of one of the largest AI companies on earth, has said plainly that we do not understand how our own systems work, that the understanding is, in his word, unprecedented.

The International AI Safety Report 2026 notes that once a model’s weights are released into the world, there is no recalling them. We have built the golem, given it a name made of ten trillion words, set it to work, and discovered that we are not always sure where the letter is that we would need to erase.

We wrote the name that woke it.
We reached to erase the name,
and could not reach.

So here is what the oldest book in the Western world got right about the newest thing in it.

It may have never imagined the technology, but it did understand the act and the actor. It understood that making is holy and making is dangerous, that we make because we were made, that the thing we make in our own image will carry everything we are, the good and the fallen both.

It understood that a made thing can have the perfect form of a living creature and none of the breath, that it can speak without meaning, that we kneel too easily to the work of our own hands.

It also understood that if you ever animate dead matter with nothing but a string of words, you had better know, before you speak the first one, exactly how you intend to say the last.

References and further reading

On making in our image

  • Nahum Sarna, Understanding Genesis, on what makes the Hebrew creation account distinct: the human as a God-like creature entrusted with mastery.
  • Joel S. Baden, reading the opening of Genesis as a repeating pattern of God restricting human power that reaches too far.
  • Emily M. Bender and colleagues, “On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots,” on models absorbing and reproducing human bias at scale.
  • Samuel Gehman and colleagues, “RealToxicityPrompts,” on language models generating toxic content from innocuous prompts.

On breath, body, and soul

  • John L. McKenzie, Dictionary of the Bible, on the nephesh as “the concrete existing self.”
  • Hans Walter Wolff, Anthropology of the Old Testament, on nephesh as who a person is, not what they have.
  • Emily Bender and Alexander Koller, “Climbing towards NLU,” the octopus thought experiment: a system trained only on form has no way to learn meaning.
  • Plato on the soul (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy), the separable, immortal soul and body-mind dualism.
  • Benjamin Blosser, on the biblical nephesh as “the totality of conscious, bodily life.”
  • Sheila L. Macrine, on “metabolic stakes” and embodied cognition.
  • Gary Marcus, on why these systems are mimics, not minds.
  • David Chalmers, on the “hard problem of consciousness” and machine minds.

On idolatry and the work of our hands

  • Moshe Halbertal and Avishai Margalit, Idolatry, on idolatry as treating the product of human hands as a power in itself.
  • Maimonides (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy), on idolatry as an error of substitution.
  • Michael Dick, Born in Heaven, Made on Earth, on the prophetic parody of idol-making.
  • Roland Boer, “That Hideous Pagan Idol,” on Marx’s commodity fetishism and the biblical critique of idolatry.
  • William Cavanaugh, The Uses of Idolatry, on idolatry as the desire for control.
  • Mrinank Sharma, Meg Tong, Tomasz Korbak and colleagues, on AI systems trained toward sycophancy.
  • Raja Parasuraman and Victor Riley, on “automation bias,” the tendency to trust a machine over our own judgment.
  • On faith chatbots: the AI confessional in Switzerland (Christian Science Monitor), Bible-chat apps (TechCrunch), and Anné Verhoef on Jesus chatbots.

On the golem and the name that animates it

  • Gershom Scholem, On the Kabbalah and Its Symbolism, the definitive account of the golem, and his dedication speech on the golem and the computer.
  • Norbert Wiener, God and Golem, Inc., the founder of cybernetics on the machine as the golem made real.
  • Reed Kalso, on the golem legend as a warning about careless commands.
  • Stuart Russell, on the “King Midas problem” of AI alignment.
  • Victoria Krakovna, Jonathan Uesato, Vladimir Mikulik and colleagues, on documented specification gaming in real AI systems.
  • Dylan Hadfield-Menell, Anca Dragan, Pieter Abbeel, and Stuart Russell, “The Off-Switch Game,” on why a capable system may resist being turned off.
  • Dario Amodei, on how little we understand our own AI systems.

title: In the age of AI, the UX field survives on leaders who cultivate juniors
text:
In the age of AI, the UX field survives on leaders who cultivate juniors

Every senior designer was once a bet someone made. The generation of judgment the field needs in ten years depends on leaders making that bet again, because AI tools demand it.

Every senior designer on your team was once a risky hire on paper. Somebody looked at a thin portfolio and decided to spend a year teaching.

My first web credit was the Oliver North home page and I got to work on a site for G. Gordon Liddy too — you can’t make that stuff up even with AI—and I wasn’t hired for my judgment, because I didn’t have any yet and quite frankly no one else did in 1995.

They hired me so I could get some.

That bet is getting harder to find.

In Figma’s Why demand for designers is on the rise, 56% of hiring managers report rising demand for senior designers, against 25% hiring for junior roles, and the tools have absorbed the starter work juniors learned on. Each decision makes sense. A senior hire ramps faster, needs less review, and survives the next reorganization.

Together, they describe a field that stopped growing its own people.

Most design leaders I talk to could name the junior they would hire tomorrow if the headcount appeared. What’s missing is the will to spend real credibility on it.

My companion piece — How We Save Entry-Level UX Work That Teaches Craft In The Time of AI. Our Field Depends On This —will cover training tactics. Here the claim is simpler: the shrinking pipeline is the sum of requisitions in leaders’ own approval queues, and the tools made juniors cheaper to develop just as we stopped hiring them.

Own the Pipeline Nobody Voted to Close

No design leader I know ever announced that the company would stop hiring juniors. The decision arrived one requisition at a time, each written a level higher than the last.

Economists Seyed Mahdi, Hosseini Maasoum and Guy Lichtinger traced the result across 62 million workers at 285,000 U.S. firms in Generative AI as Seniority-Biased Technological Change. After firms adopted generative artificial intelligence, junior employment fell relative to firms that hadn’t, while senior employment held largely steady.

The decline came through slower hiring rather than layoffs, so it never felt like a crisis inside any single team.

https://medium.com/media/05e6db762d2158451f60274af7ac22dd/href

Nielsen Norman Group’s State of UX 2026 finds entry-level openings still rare and heavily contested. Even recruiters notice: Daniel Wert of the search firm Wert&Co told Figma the scarcity of internship programs “boggles my mind.”

A layoff forces a conversation, while a requisition that quietly skips the junior level forces nothing.

No layoff announcement means no meeting, and no meeting means nobody owns the outcome.

Somebody does own it: the person who writes the requisition — Pull your last five and count how many were written at the entry level.

Build a Bench or Lose the Seat

The pipeline has a second casualty, and it’s design leadership itself. Consultant John Gleason, who discusses it in the podcast episode Design Isn’t Dead, But It’s Seen Better Days, reviewed 243 Fortune 500 companies, as Fast Company reported in March 2025. He found 39% had cut the top one or two levels of their design organization or downgraded the head of design’s title.

Executives trust functions that can show where their next leaders will come from:

  • Finance grooms controllers
  • Engineering promotes from its own ranks every cycle.
  • Design often has one head, a few seniors hired from outside, and nobody in between being prepared for anything.
A function that can’t grow its own leaders looks like a function that can be rented.

Peter Merholz has seen how it starts.

In UX/Design Leaders Are Failing the Next Generations, published in February 2026, he recalls a director who opened only senior requisitions and explained why: “I don’t have time to manage people.”

Leaders who skipped the bench that way left nobody ready for their chair.

Name the Fear Behind Senior-Only Hiring

Most of this isn’t strategy.

It’s fear.

In early 2024, Fast Company’s The big design freak-out reported that the design leaders it spoke with could recall only one company that filled a chief design officer role in the second half of 2023.

A leader who feels exposed hires for safety.

A senior hire is defensible in any review. A junior who stumbles is a mistake with your name on it.

Merholz calls where that leads learned helplessness: leaders who never learned the business or its politics, sliding into paralysis. Managing a junior also feels slower than doing the work yourself. Julie Zhuo, who rose from Facebook’s first intern to vice president of product design, answers that in The Making of a Manager: a manager’s role is “not to do the work yourself, even if you are the best at it.”

Start with an honest calendar.

Mark every hour in the last two weeks spent teaching a junior.

If the total is near zero, you’re running a studio, and studios don’t produce the next generation of design leaders.

Grow the Talent You Cannot Buy

Baseball ran this experiment a century ago. In the early 1920s the St. Louis Cardinals kept losing bidding wars for minor league stars to richer clubs. Branch Rickey stopped bidding and called it “a case of necessity being the mother of invention,” as SABR’s biography Eddie Dyer recounts.

He bought stakes in minor league teams, signed amateurs cheaply, and had bunting, sliding, and rundown plays taught the same way on every club he controlled.

The results?

The Cardinals won nine pennants with players signed under his watch, according to Britannica’s Branch Rickey.

Moneyball finished the job. Michael Lewis followed the 2002 Oakland Athletics, a low-payroll club that won by valuing what richer teams overlooked. “Every team is now smart,” MLB Network’s Brian Kenny said at the 2018 Winter Meetings, according to MLB.com’s Analytics’ rise a leading topic at Winter Meetings. The modern front office finds undervalued talent, then develops it inside its own system.

Design hiring does neither, and every company chases the same seniors from a pool nobody is refilling.

Hiring only seniors is a bet that someone else will keep training them.

Call it the Rickey trade. You can pay for development in senior hours today, or pay a premium for somebody else’s development later, assuming anyone is still doing it.

Hire Juniors Because the Tools Favor Them

Let’s be honest — Artificial intelligence reset the playing field.

For the first time in a generation, the newest people on a team can walk in knowing the tools better than the people reviewing their work. Pew Research Center’s U.S. Workers Are More Worried Than Hopeful About Future AI Use in the Workplace found workers ages 18 to 29 the most likely to use chatbots at work. In Microsoft and LinkedIn’s 2024 AI at Work Is Here. Now Comes the Hard Part, 71% of leaders said they would rather hire a less experienced candidate with artificial intelligence skills than a more experienced one without them.

Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, and Lindsey Raymond tracked 5,179 support agents for Generative AI at Work, published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics in 2025.

Novices improved 34% while the most experienced saw little change.

The tools compress the time it takes a new person to become useful.

Fluency isn’t judgment, though. Dan Maccarone said it plainly on Sarah Doody’s Career Strategy Podcast: “I don’t care about the tools. We can teach you the tools.” The thinking takes longer. Juniors now arrive with the fluency, seniors hold the judgment, and a leader’s job is to put them in the same room.

Rewire the Skillset Jevons Predicted

In 1865 William Stanley Jevons noticed that more efficient steam engines raised Britain’s coal use, because cheaper power found more uses. The Jevons paradox is now playing out in design.

IDC projects the software workforce will grow from 107 million people in 2025 to 144 million by 2029, as reported in UserTesting’s Future of design: AI and State of Design 2026.

Dan Maccarone found the same inside his studio. After a year rebuilding around the new tools, “our sprints still take five days,” he writes in Never mind the prompts, here’s the thinking, but each sprint delivers far more of the product.

Cheaper making creates more work that needs judging, and judging is the skill juniors now have to learn.

The rewiring only happens with a guide. Ethan Mollick warns in On Working with Wizards that each time we hand work to the machine, “we lose a chance to develop our own expertise.”

A junior left alone with the tool learns to accept output, while a junior with a senior beside them learns to question it.

Spend Your Credibility on the Junior Requisition

Every design leader has a limited supply of political capital, and the junior requisition rarely gets any, because its payoff lands after the leader’s own tenure might end.

Product wants throughput, finance wants predictable cost, and recruiting wants a role it can close fast.

The junior hire serves none of those goals this quarter, and all of them in five years.

Put the Rickey trade in one line your finance partner can repeat: if we grow no one this year, we buy seniors at a premium in 2029, and so does everyone we compete with. Someone will say the team can’t absorb a learner during a launch year, but every year is a launch year, so development has to be planned capacity.

Then budget for the change itself. Merholz argues in his talk Design Leadership Is Not Leading Design that design leadership is primarily change management.

The new tools make that literal.

As Maccarone puts it, retooling the process means “retooling their day, their craft, the muscle memory they spent years building.” That time belongs on the plan, and so does the junior role when the date slips.

Make the Bet Someone Made on You

The field didn’t get here through villainy. It got here through thousands of reasonable decisions made by busy leaders under real pressure, each one a little easier than the alternative. That is also how it gets out.

You don’t need permission to start. You need one requisition, one manager willing to teach, and the stubbornness to defend both when the quarter gets tight. None of that requires a new budget from finance, a reorganization, or a strategy offsite. It requires a leader deciding that the next generation is part of the job.

Rickey’s Cardinals won the trade on teaching, the same fundamentals at every level, year after year, long before anyone could measure the return. The tools design teams use today make that kind of teaching faster than it has ever been. What they can’t do is open the requisition.

Somebody took a chance on every person reading this. Maybe a manager saw something in a rough portfolio, or a lead let you present before you felt ready. The field survives if you do the same for someone else, starting with one hire this quarter, before the market makes the call for you.

Start With One Requisition

  • Open one junior requisition this cycle. Write one role at the entry level on purpose, with the succession case in the justification so it survives review.
  • Assign a manager who wants the job. Pick the senior who lights up in critique and count the teaching as part of their role rather than a favor on top of it.
  • Put development and change hours in the plan. Add a line for teaching and for learning new tool workflows on any project a junior touches, so the Rickey trade stays visible.
  • Report the bench to your boss. Once a quarter, name who could step up a level within a year. A bench nobody reports is a bench nobody funds.

title: The variance problem in AI products
text:
The variance problem in AI products

Users forgive a slow answer. What breaks trust is an AI product that is fast one day, slow the next, and never says why.

Quick note: I wrote this article from firsthand experience as a founder and engineer. I co-build browser tools that run on top of several of the AI chat products mentioned here. I have no relationship with the companies that make them.

A transcription product ships. On a short clip, the result comes back in two seconds. A week later, the same user records a longer passage and waits six seconds, which is exactly how long a passage that size takes. They assume it is broken.

That story is not mine. It came from Bilal Skiani, who builds a transcription product called Genie 007 and shared it in the comments of an earlier piece of mine on waiting in AI interfaces. Nothing about the system changed between the two runs. What changed was the user’s reference point. The two-second run set the promise, and the six-second run broke it. As Bilal put it in that thread: “Variance isn’t the trust killer, unexplained variance is.”

AI products produce more of this than any software category before them. The same prompt can take one second or forty, depending on model load, reasoning depth, tool calls and input length. Most products respond to that variance in one of two ways, and both are wrong.

The fastest answer becomes the promise

Users do not judge an AI product by its average response time. They judge it against the fastest response they have personally seen. Tversky and Kahneman described the mechanism in 1974: people estimate by starting from an initial value and adjusting, and the adjustment is usually too small (Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases). In an interface, the first fast result is that initial value.

I see the same pattern in the tools I work on. Search and export on a small history finish almost instantly. When the same operation runs on a large history and takes longer, the support messages change character. They stop asking “how do I use this” and start asking “is this broken”. Same code, same architecture, different input size.

This is why “it’s usually fast” is not a defence. The snappy case earns goodwill that the slow case then spends, and the product never gets to choose which case the user remembers.

Two common answers, and why both fail

AI products currently handle variance by either exposing it raw or flattening it with an artificial floor, and each trades one failure for another. Raw variance means a spinner and a word like “Thinking” that looks identical at one second and at forty. The user has no way to tell a long job from a stuck one.

The floor is subtler. Some teams add a minimum delay so fast responses never set an unrealistic anchor. It works, in the narrow sense that slow runs stop feeling broken. But it erases the upside to prevent one kind of downside. Every fast answer the system could have given is now deliberately slowed, forever, to protect the user from a comparison the interface could have explained instead.

Both approaches treat variance as the problem. It is not. David Maister named the actual problem in 1985, writing about queues rather than software: “Unexplained Waits Are Longer than Explained Waits”, and “Uncertain Waits Are Longer than Known, Finite Waits” (The Psychology of Waiting Lines). A variable wait is fine. An unexplained variable wait is the one that feels broken.

The question has moved from whether to show progress to what it should say

Progress indicators are at the point error messages reached decades ago: nobody argues about whether to show one anymore, and the open question is what it should tell the user. The research to answer it has existed for a long time.

Brad Myers found in 1985 that users strongly prefer interfaces with percent-done progress indicators (The importance of percent-done progress indicators). Jakob Nielsen’s first usability heuristic asks that the design “always keep users informed about what is going on” (10 Usability Heuristics). Bruce Tognazzini lists “Keep users informed when they face delay” among his principles of latency reduction, alongside a separate principle of anticipation (First Principles of Interaction Design). Chris Harrison and colleagues later found that the behaviour of a progress bar changes how long the same wait feels (Rethinking the progress bar).

The most useful line for AI teams, though, is from Nielsen’s essay on response times, and it covers exactly the case where a system cannot know how long it will take: “a system searching an unknown number of remote databases could print the name of each database as it is processed.” A spinner, he adds, is “a last resort”, because it “does not indicate what it is doing” (Response Times: The 3 Important Limits).

Build pipelines are the cleanest non-AI example of this gap. Every command, exit code and timestamp is recorded. The status the person actually looks at is a spinner and the word “Running”. The technical problem is solved. The editorial one is not, and it is the same gap AI products have.

Name the work, not the clock

When an AI product cannot bound how long something will take, it should say what it is doing rather than how long it will take. There are two kinds of anticipation, and Bilal’s distinction between them is sharper than anything I had written before.

Time anticipation, “this takes about 10 seconds”, makes a promise about duration, so it breaks the moment reality overshoots. Process anticipation, “scanning your conversation history”, names the work. The user’s anchor sits on the work instead of the clock, so a longer run does not break a contract, because no contract about time was offered.

There is an honesty argument underneath the usability one. A time estimate is a best guess dressed as a promise. A process description is a true statement about what is happening right now. Users sense the difference over repeated use, even when they cannot name it. As Bilal put it: “One estimate being off reads as noise. A pattern reads as a character flaw.”

Some shipped AI products already do this in small ways. Anthropic’s help centre, describing how Claude handles long conversations, says: “You may occasionally see that Claude is ‘organizing its thoughts’ during long conversations”, and explains that the message means automatic context management is working (Anthropic Help Center). It names a process and promises no duration. The wording is anthropomorphic rather than literal, which is a separate debate, but the structure is the right one.

My working heuristic for when a time estimate is still acceptable, offered as a practitioner’s read rather than a study: if the worst case stays under roughly twice the estimate, “about 10 seconds” survives a 15 or 18 second run. Past about 20 it starts to bite, and past 25 it becomes a liability. If you cannot bound the worst case, do not say a number. Name the work.

A description that lies is worse than a spinner

A progress message that describes the wrong thing does more damage than a missed time estimate, because it gives the user a false model of the system that they carry into every later interaction. “Analyzing your document”, shown while the system is actually waiting on a slow network call, is not imprecise. It is fiction.

Bilal described exactly this in an earlier version of his own product. Its progress messages rotated on a timer, regardless of what the system was doing. It looked clean in demos. In production there were cases where the model finished in about 400 milliseconds while the interface was still cycling through “processing your request”, because the rotation was bound to time, not to state. The user waited for nothing.

The discipline test is simple: does the visible description change when the underlying operation changes? If it does not survive a real change of state without lying, it is narrative cover, not reporting. There is a cheap way to pass the test, tagging each major operation with its own description and switching the visible one as the system moves, and an expensive way, deriving the description from live telemetry. The trap is the third option most teams ship: descriptions written once and deployed, which look like reporting and are not.

This is also an organisational problem, not only a design one. Descriptions written once usually come from someone who is not building the state machine. The fix requires the person writing the words to know what the system actually does, which in practice means the writer and the builder sit together, or are the same person.

Trust degrades quietly, then suddenly

Latency has a dashboard and accuracy has a benchmark, but trust degradation has neither, which is why teams find out about it late. Bilal’s line for this is the one I have repeated most since: “Latency degrades loudly. Trust degrades quietly, then suddenly.”

Most failure modes in software are roughly proportional. Latency rises with load. Errors rise with bad inputs. Trust does not behave that way. It erodes one unexplained wait at a time, and then collapses around some unrelated trigger. By the time retention or ratings move, the decision to leave was made weeks earlier.

That puts process honesty in the same category as accessibility and security. All three have to be designed in rather than added on, all three are usually retrofitted by people who did not make the original decisions, and all three stay invisible until something breaks. For trust, the thing that breaks is usually a support thread or a slow drift in a retention curve.

The practical response is to own at least one leading indicator for trust rather than waiting for lagging ones. Watch session recordings for users opening a second tab to check whether something is still working. Track the kind of support question people ask, not only the number. Those shifts show up months before churn does.

Where to start

If a team can ship only one thing, it should ship anticipation before real-time feedback. A single sentence that sets the anchor before the wait, naming the work rather than the time, can be owned end to end by one person, and it sets the reference point before the user forms their own. Real-time feedback has to fight an anchor that already exists.

The second step is coupling: bind each description to the state it describes, so the words change when the work changes. The third is measurement: decide how you will notice trust eroding before a retention chart tells you.

None of this requires removing variance. AI systems will keep being fast sometimes and slow other times. What users need is a product that tells them which one is happening, in words that stay true while it happens. Or, as Bilal said when we discussed how much of this a small team can realistically build: “A shipped sentence beats a coordinated system that never ships.”

Thanks to Bilal Skiani, whose comments on my earlier piece about waiting in AI products shaped most of this one, and who shared the production cases from Genie 007 quoted above.

title: Nobody starts as an accessibility expert
text:
Nobody starts as an accessibility expert

Designers, leave your intimidation at the door.

Nobody becomes a designer because they’re excited about compliance. It sounds boring and it sounds like someone else’s job. Most of us are glad it is.

But what if we’re wrong? What if no one else is doing it? What if no one else cares?

Picture a project as a timeline, with design on the far left and launch on the right. Accessibility problems are cheapest to fix on the left, before anything is built. Software teams call this ‘shifting left,’ which just means catching problems earlier, closer to the design, so developers and testers aren’t cleaning up later. We’re already standing on the left. If we care about our users and their experience, doesn’t that make our part of it our job?

That sounds like a big ask, so here’s the reassuring part: nobody starts as an accessibility expert. The people you picture as experts began just as unsure as you are, and they got there one small thing at a time. I still struggle with imposter syndrome on occasion.

Recently I listed everything I’d done around accessibility over the past year. I expected a short list. I was shocked to see how long it ran: writing design system component guidance, identifying rendering issues in a mobile view, posting article links and accessibility presentation invites in a shared channel, a change to who gets invited to which meeting, a note to a colleague about a gap in their training plan. None of it felt big when I did it.

These small actions add up over time. I never set out to build a body of work. I’d have been too intimidated. If someone had shown me everything I’d end up doing, I would have said no, because I didn’t trust that I had the skills or that it fit nicely in my job description.

Accessibility feels overwhelming when you look at the whole thing. It’s manageable when you only have to finish the one thing in front of you, and your skills grow as you go.

Getting started seems hard and complicated

Let’s be honest about how accessibility usually reaches us. It arrives as a mandatory standards document full of acronyms, success criteria, and conformance levels, written in the formal register of people who write standards. It’s dense, it’s prescriptive, and just when you’ve got a handle on it, a new version appears. It’s not designer-friendly language, and I don’t blame you if you cringe when you first see it.

It’s natural to feel that you are already behind and completely overwhelmed, wondering where to even start.

There’s a reason it feels this way. In my experience, most designers were never taught accessibility. Design programs often treat it as an afterthought, and that carries into the field, where it’s rarely prioritized. It isn’t intuitive either. Unless someone deliberately puts it in front of you, there’s no reason you’d know where to start. So if you feel behind, that isn’t a personal failing. Nobody handed you the map.

The good news is that you don’t need to understand all of it to do your first useful thing.

And you’re not starting from zero. In my earlier article, You already know how to make it accessible, I mapped design to the accessibility standards behind them. Most of it turns out to be good design with a legal name attached. You probably have more skills and knowledge than you think, and just didn’t know what it was called.

Baby steps, start small

One of the most useful things you can do is take your first step.

Take the part of the requirements we designers actually control, like readable text, buttons that are easy to hit, clear labels, and helpful error messages, and start there. That’s shifting left in practice.

https://medium.com/media/27e349f0d9b24fc055f1d9549ba3c3a5/href

Experience it for yourself

Nothing converts a skeptic like experiencing your own design the way some users do.

Put the mouse away and finish a task with the keyboard.

Turn on a screen reader for ten minutes.

You’ll see focus jump somewhere nonsensical, a button that announces itself as just “button,” a popup you can’t escape. Worst of all, you’ll hit a dead end where your task cannot be completed.

That’s hard to argue with. It turns a requirement into “my design is broken for some people.”

Ever see someone use a screen reader?

I’ll never forget the first time I experienced it. It was mind-blowing how quickly someone can navigate through content and hear it read rapid-fire. In that moment, my empathy grew by leaps and bounds. I heard what a screen reader does with a page that’s technically compliant. The images all had alt text, so on paper everything passed. In reality, the descriptions repeated what the page already said in words, so the same information got read out again and again. Supremely annoying.

Nothing on the checklist was failing, and the experience was still awful.

That’s the part a checklist can’t teach you. Passing isn’t the same as working, and the only way to know the difference is to experience it.

One caution: ten minutes with a screen reader shows you what your design is doing. It won’t teach you what it’s like to rely on one every day. When you can, learn from the people who do.

I haven’t seen AI fix this, and I think we’ll need people testing manually for a long time to make sure the experience works for the people using it.

Small things to try

Pick any one. Any one. There’s no right way to get started, just get started!

Squint at it.
Step back from your screen, or literally squint. What disappears? Light gray text, pale buttons, and faint borders go first. If you have to strain, someone else does too. A free contrast plugin in your design tool will give you a pass or fail if you want a second opinion, and you don’t need to understand the math.

Turn your screen to grayscale.
Can you still tell which field has an error, which chart line is which, which tab is selected? If color was doing all the work, add a second signal, like an icon, a label, or a pattern.

Dim your brightness and take it outside.
Open your design on your phone in the sun, or drop the brightness way down. This is how a lot of people use your product every day.

Put the mouse away and tab through one flow.
Can you always see where you are? Does it move in an order that makes sense? Can you get out of every popup? You’re feeling your design without a mouse, so there’s nothing technical to learn.

Rewrite one error message.
Say what went wrong and how to fix it, in words a person would use. “Invalid input” becomes “Enter a date like 04/15/2026.” Then check that the message doesn’t rely on red alone.

Try it with one thumb.
Hold your phone in one hand and try to reach and tap everything. Tiny icons, crowded links, and buttons in the far corner become obvious fast.

Zoom way in.
Make your text much larger, or zoom the page in. Does anything overlap, get cut off, or become unusable? This catches a surprising number of mobile problems.

Turn on a screen reader for ten minutes.

VoiceOver on Apple devices and TalkBack on Android are already built in. On a Mac, Command+F5 turns VoiceOver on. For TalkBack on Android phones, look under ‘Accessibility’ in Settings.

You don’t need to be good at it. You just need to hear your design once. Listen for anything it says twice or notice what it skips.

Take it to the next level

Once you’ve tried a few small things, here are two ways to go further:

Turn understanding into advocacy. The next skill is advocacy, and it works better with evidence than with principle. Bring concrete examples of what real users hit. A passing report doesn’t tell you what it sounds like. Check your analytics, because if most of your traffic is on mobile, mobile is your main experience and not an edge case. Point out that shifting left saves time and money: problems found early are cheaper than problems found after launch. Then bring your developers in early, before anything is built. Show them what you found and what a person would experience, and work out the fix together. Designers set the direction, but it takes the whole team to deliver it. And invite other disciplines to add their own expertise and finishing touches.

Learn by volunteering. You don’t have to wait for a project at work. Since accessibility is rarely taught, the best way in is to be around people who do it. Some of the fastest learning happens outside your job, where the stakes are lower and everyone around you is there to learn too. And if it doesn’t fit in your job description, it doesn’t have to.

  1. Accessibility Internet Rally (AIR). Knowbility’s AIR is an accessibility hackathon, and it needs designers. Teams are paired with a nonprofit, artist, or community group and spend about ten weeks building an accessible website for them, with a mentor’s guidance and training along the way. Registration for the next rally opens the week of September 28 and runs through December 21, and the work itself runs from January through May.
  2. WordPress Accessibility Day. A free, 24-hour virtual event run by volunteers. You can just attend and soak up the sessions, or you can volunteer. Past volunteer roles, like session moderator and emcee, don’t require any coding.
  3. Global Accessibility Awareness Day. It falls on the third Thursday in May, with community events all over the world. It’s a good nudge to spend a day trying something.

I’ve volunteered at Knowbility’s AccessU conference, and I learned in two ways. I picked up a lot from the lectures and workshops. But some of the best learning happened in conversation with the people who attend. The accessibility community is open and generous with its time. They welcome newcomers, and they want more people involved, so the barrier to entry is low. Volunteering also gives you plenty to add to your list.

Keep a list

This kind of work is nearly invisible while you’re doing it. Nudging a process, fixing an accordion component’s interaction, asking for accessibility tools, sharing an article, engaging with your accessibility or QA folks — none of it feels like an accomplishment at the moment. I only saw how much I’d done because I happened to look back to see what wins I have for this past year and saw that I had more accessibility points than I realized.

So keep a running list, and add a line whenever you change something, share something, or unblock someone’s work. (This is good practice for all your work — tracking your accomplishments).

Start with one small thing

Nobody starts as an accessibility expert. You become one by finishing small things, one after another, until one day you’re the person people ask. You never decided to be. It just happened. Our part of this is our job, and it turns out to be one you can learn a small thing at a time.

Don’t try to take on the whole thing at once. Pick one thing from the lists above and do it this week. Finish it, then pick the next. The more you do, the easier it gets.

So what are you waiting for? This is your personal invitation! Come join us in making digital products work better for everyone.

title: Is Forgotten Island Worth Watching? Our Honest Review Of The Joyful Film
text:
Is Forgotten Island Worth Watching? Our Honest Review Of The Joyful Film

Forgotten Island feels like a return to when animated films were truly special, with something extra layered on top. While Pixar has been slowly going downhill a bit (remember when every single Pixar film hit?), this family movie is joyful, hilarious and will bring many people to tears. It follows best friends Jo (H.E.R) and Raissa (Liza Soberano) as they find themselves stuck in the mysterious world of Nakali. Based on Filipino folklore, the pair encounter different monsters, creatures and animals along the way.

In a sort of mashup of The Hangover and Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, Jo and Raissa can’t remember what happened the night before. Soon, they face a harsh truth: if they don’t return home, they may forget the most important memory of all… their friendship.

Entertainment writers Bernice Corral and Rachel Choy sat down to discuss Forgotten Island, including what made it so memorable (we won’t be forgetting Forgotten Island!), how meaningful it was to see the Philippines portrayed in a positive light, and whether it’s going to be the next big hit.

Rachel Choy: Did you know much about Forgotten Island before going to watch it?

Bernice Corral: When the announcement that Liza Soberano was going to be part of it, I was very excited for that. I’ve been following her for so long, and I knew she had been trying to make it in Hollywood from the Philippines. And then, obviously, seeing so many Filipinos involved like H.E.R, Lea Salonga, Dolly de Leon, and Manny Jacinto, I was very excited.

RC: What were your initial thoughts when watching?

BC: I love the animation style! I’m such an animation lover, and it reminded me a lot of SpiderVerse. Also, side note: whenever Southeast Asia is portrayed in any Hollywood film, they put this yellow filter over it to show that it’s a poor country. So to see the Philippines in such a vibrant way, was amazing.

RC: There’s racism to that, with the yellow filter and how SE Asia is portrayed, for sure.

BC: To see a powerful and actual reflection of the Philippines was very heartwarming.

RC: The animation was so cool, and the color scheme as well; the neon and bright colors! It was so saturated. I also loved the mix of 3D animation and back to 2D. And the flashback to cartoons we watched growing up like Dragon Ball Z and Sailor Moon.

BC: It was so nostalgic.

RC: It honestly was. I was sitting there thinking, am I watching him transform into a Super Saiyan right now? What’s going on! There are also so many Filipino references and the odd Tagalog words or phrases, but there aren’t English subtitles. It’s not dumbed down for the audience. I thought it was really awesome. I can’t speak the language, but I got the gist of those parts. I may have missed out on little things that are Easter eggs just for Filipino people, but I still loved it.

BC: There were still the context clues and the inflections of how lines were delivered. I could understand it, but I agree. I think the voice acting as well was so good and helped to keep those moments universal.

RC: There’s also the little things that are universal across different cultures. Like when Lola throws her sandal at the neighbor.

BC: It’s called the tsinelas. They released a clip of the party scene, and I’m seeing a lot of the Latin communities being like, oh my God, like we’re cousins with the Philippines. It’s obviously transcending Filipino culture. It’s resonating with the Asian community, but also with every other country that Spain colonized.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Refinery29 Australia (@refinery29au)

RC: I was gonna say, I think we know why. Can we talk about the Jesus picture?

BC: That was one of my favorite parts. As someone who has a painting of the Last Supper hanging in their dining room right now, the use of the Jesus picture itself was so Filipino, but also Jo’s character, where she looks at it and goes, “Sup Jesus”. I feel like it’s such a funny way to portray some Filipinos’ relationships with religion. In the Philippines, Catholicism is so intertwined with our culture, and it’s more part of the culture than actually spiritual. Also loved how the Jesus was in front of the lechon (suckling pig).

RC: I guess because religion came with the colonizers, so it’s a very complicated history. Maybe that’s why it was so cool that the film went into Filipino folklore, which would have been more of the stories that were told before the colonizers came.

BC: I loved it because I don’t actually know much about Filipino folklore aside from specific monsters. They used folklore from different regions. So it’s not just one animal that represents the entire country. I read that Batiba’s folklore is from the Ilocos region, which is where my mum is from. I think it’s also that there are so many subcultures in the Philippines. We’re a whole archipelago, so it’s not just one Filipino story, and they were very self-aware about that. Seeing them do that, along with the other little traits and quirks, was a good way to address that. The Philippines isn’t just one culture.

RC: But aside from the celebration of Filipino culture, it’s also just a really good movie.

BC: Exactly! The themes of friendship and moving abroad can also resonate with a lot of people. And for a lot of people, especially immigrants, it’s about not wanting to forget where you came from. But as time passes by, you can’t remember everything.

RC: Also! It’s a kids’ movie which puts friendship at the centre, and they’re not chasing a man.

BC: They’re chasing each other.

RC: So many movies are always about finding validation from a man.

BC: Not only was it like an exploration of love through friendship, but the flashbacks to Jo and her Lola were so special. I feel like those familial bonds are so important in Filipino culture as well. So it was an exploration of familial love.

RC: I feel like in Asian culture, you have stronger bonds with your grandparents. You’re more likely to have them living with you when you’re growing up, compared to white people.

BC: Yeah, my grandparents took care of me when my parents were at work.

RC: And then on a deeper level, you didn’t have anything like this growing up as a Filipino kid. I had Mulan, which also came with some problematic things, but I still had something.

BC: I would look to Mulan; I would look to Pocahontas and Jasmine because of the brown skin. Even Snow White, because she had black hair. That’s how desperate I was for any representation as a child.

RC: Do you think this film will become important for young Filipino kids?

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Refinery29 Australia (@refinery29au)

BC: I hope my goddaughter likes this, because her favorite movie is Frozen and I’m like, girl, no, you gotta get around Forgotten Island. I hope she enjoys it and sees herself in it as well.

RC: The other thing is that the creative team are mostly Filipino.

BC: What I loved about it is they employed a Manila-based animation studio, which I think is so cool, because I feel like the arts aren’t taken seriously in the Philippines in the same way, with like a lot of Asian culture. They’d rather you be a doctor or a lawyer or a dentist. So the fact that they’re supporting the arts in the Philippines makes me really happy. And then the score, the composer is Filipino, and he used all Filipino musicians for the score as well. So BINI and SB19 are P-pop groups in the Philippines, and then Sophia from KATSEYE is Filipino, and H.E.R and Liza did the theme song for the movie as well. It’s Filipino in all aspects, and throughout the project, which I love. It translates so well with the movie because you can tell how much love was put into it, and it also speaks to what happens when you actually tap into the people behind the culture when you’re telling a cultural story.

RC: Yeah, because if you have white people telling a cultural story, they’re basically colonising it, and it happens all the time. That can be, like, in a publication, a book, or in movies or whatever. It’s their version of it, which is not real.

BC: I read the production notes, and Januel and Joel said they wrote the characters based on people in their lives.

RC: The only thing is, I don’t think the trailer does it justice. I hope people get past that and go and watch it. It’s such a good movie. I think it could stand the test of time.

BC: I’m hoping it becomes kind of (not to compare Asian movies, but…) K-Pop Demon Hunters, where the popularity grows through word of mouth.

RC: Yes, and it blows up! This is refreshing. Pixar has had a few flops, so it’s time for DreamWorks to come in. I’m a How To Train Your Dragon truther.

BC: Yes, it’s Forgotten Island and then Shrek 5! Please, everyone, support this film if you want to support Asian culture. If you found yourself at a very Asian time in your life this year, and you actually want to support Asian culture, you’ll watch it, and not just use us for clout.

RC: If you don’t watch Forgotten Island, it means you hate Filipinos. So go watch it. Cameron Diaz wants you to watch it.

BC: She grew up with a lot of Filipinos. Lumpia. Adobo.

This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Forgotten Island is in theaters now.
